questions.q: Why does fixed-interval retrying (e.g., always retry after exactly 1 second) make provider-side congestion worse rather than better?
options: All clients retrying on the same fixed interval synchronize into retry storms that hit the congested system simultaneously, worsening the congestion
Fixed-interval retrying is actually always optimal and the lesson recommends it
Fixed-interval retries are billed at a higher rate than exponential backoff retries
Fixed intervals cause circuits to fail validation
questions.explain: When many clients retry on the same fixed schedule, their retries pile up simultaneously on the already-congested system, worsening rather than relieving the congestion -- the core motivation for exponential backoff with jitter.

questions.q: With a base delay of 500ms and a cap of 60,000ms, what is the deterministic backoff cap for attempt 3 (0-indexed), and what is the total worst-case wait across 6 attempts (0-5)?
options: Attempt 3: 4,000 ms; total across 6 attempts: 31,500 ms (~31.5 sec)
Attempt 3: 500 ms; total across 6 attempts: 3,000 ms
Attempt 3: 60,000 ms; total across 6 attempts: 360,000 ms
Attempt 3: 8,000 ms; total across 6 attempts: 48,000 ms
questions.explain: min(60000, 500*2^3) = 4,000 ms for attempt 3. Summing 500+1000+2000+4000+8000+16000 = 31,500 ms across all 6 attempts (0 through 5).

questions.q: What does 'full jitter' add on top of the deterministic exponential backoff cap?
options: It picks the actual retry delay as a random value uniformly between 0 and the computed cap, so simultaneous retriers don't all retry in lockstep
It doubles the deterministic cap for extra safety margin
It removes the cap entirely, allowing unlimited delay growth
It replaces exponential growth with a fixed, constant delay
questions.explain: Full jitter randomizes the delay within [0, cap] for that attempt, which is what actually desynchronizes multiple clients that hit the same failure at the same time -- a plain deterministic exponential delay alone doesn't achieve that.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what are the two stopping rules a retry loop should combine, rather than relying on just one?
options: A max-attempt count AND a cumulative-time budget tied to the job's latency requirement
Only a max-attempt count, since time budgets are irrelevant to retries
Only a cumulative-cost budget, since attempt count and time don't matter
A random coin flip combined with provider approval
questions.explain: The lesson recommends combining a max-attempt count with a cumulative-time budget, since there's no point retrying past the point where a result would arrive too late to be useful, regardless of how many attempts remain.

questions.q: What is the preferred order of fallback options the lesson gives once retrying is no longer worthwhile?
options: (1) Retry on a different available device, (2) fall back to a classical simulator with a clear lower-fidelity flag, (3) explicitly fail the iteration rather than silently substituting a wrong value
(1) Silently substitute a zero value, (2) retry forever, (3) crash the whole pipeline
(1) Explicitly fail immediately with no other options considered
(1) Always fall back to a classical simulator first, before ever trying a different device
questions.explain: The lesson orders fallbacks by preference: switching devices first (often lowest cost/latency penalty), then a flagged simulator substitute, and only as a last resort an explicit failure -- never a silent, unflagged substitution, which would repeat Lesson 12's silent-corruption warning.
